23.title: Numbers, Prices, and Time of Day

questions.prompt: What does the prefix *toʻa* do in *teine e toʻalua*, and what does the chapter say of *teine e fā*?

options.label: A
options.text: It marks the number as counting people; *teine e fā*, "the four girls", counts people with the plain number, which is also used.
options.explanation: Correct: *toʻa* is the careful form for counting human beings, but it is not strictly required, and everyday speech often leaves it off.

options.label: B
options.text: It marks the number as counting people; *teine e fā*, "the four girls", is wrong, because a count of people must always take *toʻa*.
options.explanation: The prefix is not strictly required: people are also counted with the plain number, as in *teine e fā*.

options.label: C
options.text: It turns the number into a place in an order; *teine e fā*, "the four girls", counts people with the plain number, which is also used.
options.explanation: The prefix *toʻa* marks a count of human beings; it does not put things in order.

options.label: D
options.text: It marks the number as counting people; *teine e fā*, "the five girls", counts people with the plain number, which is also used.
options.explanation: The number *fā* is four, so the phrase is "the four girls".

questions.prompt: What do *ono*, *tālā*, *sene* and *ʻātoa* mean, in that order?

options.label: D
options.text: *Lē siva.*
options.explanation: Correct: this is the wrong one, because a command carries no tense particle for the not-word *lē* to follow; it is forbidden with the do-not verb instead.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the belonging words *a* and *o*?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *a* marks a relationship that is given, and *o* one the owner started and controls; the owner in an *a* phrase need not be a person; and the control rule sorts most words but not all.
options.explanation: The two jobs are the other way round: *a* marks what the owner started and controls, and *o* what is given.

options.label: B
options.text: The word *a* marks a relationship the owner started and controls, and *o* one that is given; the owner in an *a* phrase need not be a person; and the control rule sorts most words but not all.
options.explanation: Correct: control decides most words, an *a* owner is usually a person without having to be one, and the rest are learned word by word.

options.label: C
options.text: The word *a* marks a relationship the owner started and controls, and *o* one that is given; the owner in an *a* phrase must always be a person; and the control rule sorts most words but not all.
options.explanation: The owner in an *a* phrase is usually a person, because getting and using things is what people do, but it does not have to be one.

options.label: D
options.text: The word *a* marks a relationship the owner started and controls, and *o* one that is given; the owner in an *a* phrase need not be a person; and the control rule decides the belonging word of every word.
options.explanation: The control rule sorts most words, and some words sit where it does not put them, so their type is learned as a fact of the word.

questions.prompt: What do the chapter's words *atunuʻu*, *lanu*, *maʻamusa*, *paopao*, *pele*, *tao* and *ʻie* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: colour, country, lover, canoe, darling, spear, kilt
options.explanation: The first two are the wrong way round: *atunuʻu* is "country" and *lanu* is "colour".

options.label: B
options.text: country, colour, darling, canoe, lover, spear, kilt
options.explanation: The two people-words are the wrong way round: *maʻamusa* is "lover" and *pele* is "darling".

options.label: C
options.text: country, colour, lover, canoe, darling, spear, dress
options.explanation: The last word is not "dress": *ʻie* is "kilt".

options.label: D
options.text: country, colour, lover, canoe, darling, spear, kilt
options.explanation: Correct: all seven meanings stand in the order of the words.

questions.prompt: How do you say "a car of mine", "a house of mine", "some cups of mine" and "some houses of mine", in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: *saʻu taʻavale*, *soʻu fale*, *ni aʻu ipu*, *ni oʻu fale*
options.explanation: Correct: one thing of no particular identity takes *saʻu* or *soʻu*, and more than one thing of no particular identity takes *ni* in front of *aʻu* or *oʻu*.

options.label: B
options.text: *saʻu taʻavale*, *oʻu fale*, *ni aʻu ipu*, *ni oʻu fale*
options.explanation: The second form names more than one particular house, not one house of no particular identity.

options.label: C
options.text: *saʻu taʻavale*, *soʻu fale*, *aʻu ipu*, *ni oʻu fale*
options.explanation: The third form names more than one particular cup; "some" calls for *ni* in front.

options.label: D
options.text: *laʻu taʻavale*, *soʻu fale*, *ni aʻu ipu*, *ni oʻu fale*
options.explanation: The first form names one particular car, "my car"; "a car of mine" takes *saʻu*.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the words that take *a*?

options.label: A
options.text: *sipuni* (cup) and *naifi* (knife) are things got and used, and take *a*; *fānau* (children) and *pele* (darling) take *a* as well.
options.explanation: *Sipuni* is "spoon", not "cup"; the cup is *ipu*.

options.label: B
options.text: *sipuni* (spoon) and *naifi* (knife) are things got and used, and take *o*; *fānau* (children) and *pele* (darling) take *a*.
options.explanation: Things got and used take *a*, so a spoon and a knife are *a*-words.

options.label: C
options.text: *sipuni* (spoon) and *naifi* (knife) are things got and used, and take *a*; *fānau* (children) and *pele* (darling), people taken into a life, take *a* as well.
options.explanation: Correct: things got and used, one's children and the people taken into a life are all *a*-words.

options.label: D
options.text: *sipuni* (spoon) and *naifi* (knife) are things got and used, and take *a*; *fānau* (children) take *o*, as family by birth does.
options.explanation: One's children take *a*; it is family by birth, such as *tamā* (father), that takes *o*.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the words that take *o*?

options.label: A
options.text: *tamā* (father) takes *a*, but *ulu* (head), *pito* (end) and *lanu* (colour) take *o*, and so do *paopao* (canoe), *nuʻu* (village) and *igoa* (name).
options.explanation: Family by birth, such as *tamā* (father), takes *o*.

options.label: B
options.text: *tamā* (father), *ulu* (head) and *pito* (end) take *o*, but *lanu* (colour) takes *a*; *paopao* (canoe), *nuʻu* (village) and *igoa* (name) take *o*.
options.explanation: A colour is a quality of the thing itself, and takes *o*.

options.label: C
options.text: *tamā* (father), *ulu* (head), *pito* (end) and *lanu* (colour) take *o*, and so do *nuʻu* (village) and *igoa* (name), but *paopao* (canoe) takes *a*, since a boat is got and used.
options.explanation: Boats take *o*, whatever the means of getting one.

options.label: D
options.text: *tamā* (father), *ulu* (head), *pito* (end) and *lanu* (colour) all take *o*: family by birth, a part of the body, a part of a whole and a thing's own quality; and so do *paopao* (canoe), *nuʻu* (village) and *igoa* (name): a boat, the place a person lives or comes from, and a name.
options.explanation: Correct: all seven belong to groups the chapter lists as *o*-words.

questions.prompt: Where the control rule runs out, which of these is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The son of a woman takes *o* and the son of a man takes *a*; control does not explain the pair; and clothes such as *ʻie* (kilt) take *o*, as do a few traditional tools and weapons such as *tao* (spear), even though they are chosen and put to use.
options.explanation: The pair is the other way round: the son of a woman takes *a* and the son of a man takes *o*.

options.label: B
options.text: The son of a woman takes *a* and the son of a man takes *o*, and control explains the pair, because the mother started the relationship; clothes such as *ʻie* (kilt) take *o*, as do a few traditional tools and weapons such as *tao* (spear), even though they are chosen and put to use.
options.explanation: Control does not explain the pair, and no reason for it is known.

options.label: C
options.text: The son of a woman takes *a* and the son of a man takes *o*; control does not explain the pair; and clothes such as *ʻie* (kilt) take *a*, since they are chosen and put on, though a few traditional tools and weapons such as *tao* (spear) take *o*.
options.explanation: Clothes take *o*, even though a kilt is chosen and put on.

options.label: D
options.text: The son of a woman takes *a* and the son of a man takes *o*; control does not explain the pair; and clothes such as *ʻie* (kilt) take *o*, as do a few traditional tools and weapons such as *tao* (spear), even though they are chosen and put to use.
options.explanation: Correct: the same son is joined to his mother with *a* and to his father with *o*, and clothes and a few traditional tools and weapons are *o*-words although they are chosen and used.

questions.prompt: Two words in this chapter differ only in their marks, *ʻava* and *āvā*. Which of these is true of them?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *ʻava* is "wife" and *āvā* is "beard"; the beard takes *a*, though parts of the body take *o*; and a wife takes *a*.
options.explanation: The meanings are the wrong way round: the word that begins with a catch in the voice is "beard", and the one with two long vowels is "wife".

options.label: B
options.text: The word *ʻava* is "beard" and *āvā* is "wife"; the beard takes *o*, like the other parts of the body; and a wife takes *a*.
options.explanation: The beard runs the other way from the rest of the body: it takes *a*.

options.label: C
options.text: The word *ʻava* is "beard" and *āvā* is "wife"; the beard takes *a*, though parts of the body take *o*; and a wife takes *a*.
options.explanation: Correct: the marks make two different words, and both take *a*, the beard against the body-part rule and the everyday wife word.

options.label: D
options.text: The word *ʻava* is "beard" and *āvā* is "wife"; the beard takes *a*, though parts of the body take *o*; and a wife takes *o*, as family by birth does.
options.explanation: The everyday wife word is an *a*-word, so a wife takes *a*.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the for-word *mo* and the with-word *ma*?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *mo* says who something is for, the aim of an action, or how long something lasts; *ma* also means "for" when a person is handed food to eat or a thing to keep; and the pair only partly echoes the *a* and *o* split.
options.explanation: Correct: the for-word covers the one who benefits, the aim and the length of time, the with-word covers food or a thing handed over, and the echo of *a* and *o* is a resemblance, not a rule.

options.label: B
options.text: The word *mo* says who something is for or the aim of an action, but never how long something lasts; *ma* also means "for" when a person is handed food to eat or a thing to keep; and the pair only partly echoes the *a* and *o* split.
options.explanation: The for-word also gives a length of time, as in "for a week".

options.label: C
options.text: The word *mo* says who something is for, the aim of an action, or how long something lasts; *ma* never means "for", and only takes a companion along or joins two doers; and the pair only partly echoes the *a* and *o* split.
options.explanation: The with-word also means "for" when a person is handed food to eat or a thing to keep.

options.label: D
options.text: The word *mo* says who something is for, the aim of an action, or how long something lasts; *ma* also means "for" when a person is handed food to eat or a thing to keep; and *ma* goes with the *a*-words and *mo* with the *o*-words, a rule to lean on.
options.explanation: The pair only looks that way in short forms of an older written Sāmoan, now very rare, so it is a resemblance and not a rule to lean on.

questions.prompt: What do *ʻO ʻupu a le tamāloa.* and *ʻO le lā ipu.* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: Some words of the man. Their cup (the two of them).
options.explanation: With no article, the first phrase names particular words, more than one; "some" would call for *ni*.

options.label: B
options.text: The words of the man. Their cup (the two of them).
options.explanation: Correct: the missing article marks more than one particular word, and the *le* in front of *lā* counts one cup.

options.label: C
options.text: The words of the man. Their cups (the two of them).
options.explanation: The *le* in front of the pronoun counts the things, so this is one cup; more than one would leave it out.

options.label: D
options.text: The word of the man. Their cup (the two of them).
options.explanation: One word would carry the article *le*; with none, the first phrase names more than one.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the forms *aʻu* and *oʻu*, and of the phrase *ʻO le lā ipu.*?

options.label: A
options.text: The form *aʻu* is "me" wherever it stands, even in front of a naming word; *oʻu* has its catch between its two vowels; and in *ʻO le lā ipu.* the pronoun *lā* is a separate word, and with a pair of owners the belonging word is not required.
options.explanation: In front of a naming word the form is "my", as in *aʻu taʻavale*, "my cars"; only standing on its own is it "me".

options.label: B
options.text: In front of a naming word *aʻu* is "my", and on its own it is "me"; *oʻu* has its catch in the same place as the word for "I" met at the start of this book; and in *ʻO le lā ipu.* the pronoun *lā* is a separate word, and with a pair of owners the belonging word is not required.
options.explanation: The catch in the possessive form falls between the two vowels; in the word for "I" it comes first.

options.label: C
options.text: In front of a naming word *aʻu* is "my", and on its own it is "me"; *oʻu* has its catch between its two vowels; and in *ʻO le lā ipu.* the pronoun *lā* and the belonging word have folded into one word, as in *laʻu*.
options.explanation: With a pair or a group of owners the pronoun stays a separate word, and the belonging word is not required.

options.label: D
options.text: In front of a naming word *aʻu* is "my", and on its own it is "me"; *oʻu* has its catch between its two vowels; and in *ʻO le lā ipu.* the pronoun *lā* is a separate word, and with a pair of owners the belonging word is not required.
options.explanation: Correct: position decides between "my" and "me", the catch in *oʻu* sits between the vowels, and with a pair of owners the pronoun stays a separate word and the belonging word is not required.

questions.prompt: What is a spatial noun, and can the set of spatial nouns take new members?

options.label: A
options.text: A small word that works like an English preposition such as "behind", and the set takes new members freely.
options.explanation: Where English reaches for a preposition, Sāmoan uses a noun here, and the set is closed.

options.label: B
options.text: A noun that names a region of space belonging to a thing, such as its inside, its top or its back, or a direction, such as north or inland; and the set is closed: it takes no new members.
options.explanation: Correct: the spatial noun carries the meaning an English preposition would carry, the class holds the direction nouns too, and no new words join the set.

options.label: C
options.text: A noun that names a region of space belonging to a thing, such as its inside, its top or its back, or a direction, such as north or inland; and the set takes new members freely.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but the set is closed and takes no new members.

options.label: D
options.text: A small word that works like an English preposition such as "behind", and the set is closed: it takes no new members.
options.explanation: The set is closed, but a spatial noun is a noun that names a region or a direction, not a small word that works like a preposition.

questions.prompt: How do you say "The cat under the house" in Sāmoan?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻO le pusi ʻi lalo le fale.*

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻO le pusi ʻi tua o le fale.*
options.explanation: The frame is whole, but its spatial noun is not the one for "under"; that word is *lalo*.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻO le pusi ʻi lalo o le fale.*
options.explanation: Correct: the place word *ʻi*, the spatial noun *lalo*, the belonging word *o*, then the house.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻO le pusi ʻi luma o le fale.*
options.explanation: The frame is whole, but its spatial noun is not the one for "under"; that word is *lalo*.

questions.prompt: Four things are true of how the spatial-noun frame is used. Which option states all four correctly?

options.label: A
options.text: The belonging word is always *o*, because the region of a thing is given rather than got; the frame can follow a verb, naming where the action happens or where the going is headed; a direction noun can stand straight after *ʻi* with no belonging phrase; and a direction noun can also fill the whole frame, as *sisifo* does in *ʻO le nuʻu ʻi sisifo o le uafu.*
options.explanation: Correct: spatial relationships take *o* as a group of their own, the frame attaches to a verb as well as to a noun, and a direction noun can stand alone after *ʻi* or take a place in the belonging slot.

options.label: B
options.text: The belonging word is *a*; the frame can follow a verb, naming where the action happens or where the going is headed; a direction noun can stand straight after *ʻi* with no belonging phrase; and a direction noun can also fill the whole frame, as *sisifo* does in *ʻO le nuʻu ʻi sisifo o le uafu.*
options.explanation: The belonging word is *o*, never *a*, because the region of a thing is given rather than got.

options.label: C
options.text: The belonging word is always *o*; the frame follows only a noun, never a verb; a direction noun can stand straight after *ʻi* with no belonging phrase; and a direction noun can also fill the whole frame, as *sisifo* does in *ʻO le nuʻu ʻi sisifo o le uafu.*
options.explanation: The frame also follows a verb, where it names the place the action happens or, after a verb of going, the place it is headed for.

options.label: D
options.text: The belonging word is always *o*; the frame can follow a verb, naming where the action happens or where the going is headed; a direction noun after *ʻi* always needs a belonging phrase after it; and a direction noun can also fill the whole frame, as *sisifo* does in *ʻO le nuʻu ʻi sisifo o le uafu.*
options.explanation: A direction noun can stand after the place word on its own, with no belonging phrase after it.

questions.prompt: What does *ʻUa ʻi luga le pusi.* mean?

options.explanation: In front of a number the prefix counts occasions rather than things, so the boy has cried three times.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻUa tagi faʻatolu le tama.* The boy has cried three times; *Sā faʻailoa e le teine le tala.* The girl knew the story; *E leai se tagata e tū faʻamauga.* No man stands like a mountain; *Sā faʻasuka e le teine le vai.* The girl sweetened the water.
options.explanation: The built word *faʻailoa* means show, make known, so this says "The girl made the story known".

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻUa tagi faʻatolu le tama.* The boy has cried three times; *Sā faʻailoa e le teine le tala.* The girl made the story known; *E leai se tagata e tū faʻamauga.* No man stands like a mountain; *Sā faʻasuka e le teine le vai.* The girl salted the water.
options.explanation: The built word *faʻasuka* is built on *suka*, sugar, so the girl sweetened the water.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the six direction words?

options.label: A
options.text: They stand in front of the verb; *mai*, *atu* and *ane* take their bearings from the speaker, and *aʻe*, *ifo* and *ʻese* from the event itself; and the point the speaker-based words measure from is usually the speaker but can be another person or thing the speaker picks out.
options.explanation: A direction word stands after the verb, never in front of it; when the doer is named after the verb, the direction word comes in front of the doer.

options.label: B
options.text: They stand after the verb, in front of a doer named after the verb; *mai*, *atu* and *ane* take their bearings from the speaker, and *aʻe*, *ifo* and *ʻese* from the event itself; and the point the speaker-based words measure from is always the speaker and never anyone else.
options.explanation: The point is usually the speaker, but the speaker can pick out another person or thing instead, most often the one a story is following.

options.label: C
options.text: They stand after the verb, in front of a doer named after the verb; *mai*, *atu* and *ane* take their bearings from the speaker, and *aʻe*, *ifo* and *ʻese* from the event itself; and the point the speaker-based words measure from is usually the speaker but can be another person or thing the speaker picks out.
options.explanation: Correct: all three parts are what the chapter teaches about where the words stand and what fixes their direction.

options.label: D
options.text: They stand after the verb, in front of a doer named after the verb; *aʻe*, *ifo* and *ʻese* take their bearings from the speaker, and *mai*, *atu* and *ane* from the event itself; and the point the speaker-based words measure from is usually the speaker but can be another person or thing the speaker picks out.
options.explanation: The two groups are the other way round: up is up and down is down whoever is speaking, so *aʻe*, *ifo* and *ʻese* are the ones fixed by the event.

questions.prompt: What does *Na alu ʻese le tama.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The boy went off, away from me and toward you.
options.explanation: That direction is measured from the speaker, and *ʻese* is measured from a point the event itself fixes.

options.label: B
options.text: The boy went past.
options.explanation: Going past is measured from where the speaker stands, and *ʻese* is measured from a point the event itself fixes.

options.label: C
options.text: The boy went down.
options.explanation: Down is the job of a different direction word; *ʻese* says away from a point.

options.label: D
options.text: The boy went away.
options.explanation: Correct: after a verb *ʻese* means away from a point, so the boy went away.

questions.prompt: How do you say "The boy went past" in Sāmoan?

options.label: A
options.text: *Na alu atu le tama.*
options.explanation: This sets a different direction word after the verb, not the one for going past.

options.label: B
options.text: *Na alu aʻe le tama.*
options.explanation: This says the boy went up.

options.label: C
options.text: *Na alu ane le tama.*
options.explanation: Correct: *ane* is along, passing the speaker by, so the boy went past.

options.label: D
options.text: *Na alu ifo le tama.*
options.explanation: This too sets a different direction word after the verb, not the one for going past.

questions.prompt: Which option has every sentence paired with the English this chapter gives it?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻOu te lē popole atu ʻia te ʻoe.* I do not worry about you; *ʻUa maua lou faʻamalu?* Have you got your umbrella?; *Na alu ifo le tama.* The boy went down; *Faʻatali atu.* Wait here until I come back. (Lit. "Wait, away from me.")
options.explanation: Correct: *popole* is worry and *atu* turns it toward the person spoken to, *faʻamalu* is umbrella, *ifo* is down, and with *atu* the speaker is the one leaving, so the waiting is turned away from the speaker.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻOu te lē popole atu ʻia te ʻoe.* I do not worry about you; *ʻUa maua lou faʻamalu?* Have you got your handkerchief?; *Na alu ifo le tama.* The boy went down; *Faʻatali atu.* Wait here until I come back. (Lit. "Wait, away from me.")
options.explanation: *Faʻamalu* is umbrella, so the second sentence asks whether you have got your umbrella.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻOu te lē popole atu ʻia te ʻoe.* I do not worry about you; *ʻUa maua lou faʻamalu?* Have you got your umbrella?; *Na alu ifo le tama.* The boy went up; *Faʻatali atu.* Wait here until I come back. (Lit. "Wait, away from me.")
options.explanation: *Ifo* is down, so the third sentence says the boy went down.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻOu te lē popole atu ʻia te ʻoe.* I do not worry about you; *ʻUa maua lou faʻamalu?* Have you got your umbrella?; *Na alu ifo le tama.* The boy went down; *Faʻatali atu.* Wait for me. (Lit. "Wait, away from me.")
options.explanation: With *atu* the speaker is the one leaving and wants the other person to stay put, so this is "Wait here until I come back"; "Wait for me" is *Faʻatali mai*.

questions.prompt: What do the words *afi*, *leo*, *solosolo* and *tuagane* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: fire, voice, handkerchief, and brother (of a woman)
options.explanation: Correct: *afi* is fire, *leo* is voice, *solosolo* is handkerchief and *tuagane* is brother (of a woman).

options.label: B
options.text: voice, fire, handkerchief, and brother (of a woman)
options.explanation: The first two meanings are the right ones in the wrong order: *afi* is fire and *leo* is voice.

options.label: C

options.explanation: The last two meanings are the right ones in the wrong order: *solosolo* is handkerchief and *tuagane* is brother (of a woman).

options.label: D
options.text: fire, house, handkerchief, and brother (of a woman)
options.explanation: House is *fale*, the word at the end of many of this chapter's sentences; *leo* is voice.

questions.prompt: Which option pairs every word with the meaning this chapter gives it?

options.label: A
options.text: *ita*: angry, be angry; *osofaʻi*: wait; *sasao*: blaze, burn fiercely; *taʻoto*: lie (down); *popole*: worry
options.explanation: The second pairing is wrong: *osofaʻi* is attack, and wait is *faʻatali*.

options.label: B
options.text: *ita*: angry, be angry; *osofaʻi*: attack; *sasao*: blaze, burn fiercely; *taʻoto*: stand; *popole*: worry
options.explanation: The fourth pairing is wrong: *taʻoto* is lie (down).

options.label: C
options.text: *ita*: angry, be angry; *osofaʻi*: attack; *sasao*: sleep; *taʻoto*: lie (down); *popole*: worry
options.explanation: The third pairing is wrong: *sasao* is blaze, burn fiercely.

options.label: D
options.text: *ita*: angry, be angry; *osofaʻi*: attack; *sasao*: blaze, burn fiercely; *taʻoto*: lie (down); *popole*: worry
options.explanation: Correct: all five pairings are the meanings the chapter gives.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of where words stand?

options.label: A
options.text: A describing word and a direction word can both follow the verb, and the describing word comes first; the pointing-back word *ai* comes before the direction word; and inside a spatial noun phrase the direction word comes directly after the spatial noun, before the belonging word, as in *ʻi lalo ifo o le fale*.
options.explanation: The direction word comes first and *ai* after it, as in *Sā nofo aʻe ai le tama.*

options.label: B
options.text: A describing word and a direction word can both follow the verb, and the direction word comes first; the pointing-back word *ai* comes after the direction word; and inside a spatial noun phrase the direction word comes directly after the spatial noun, before the belonging word, as in *ʻi lalo ifo o le fale*.
options.explanation: The describing word comes before the direction word.

options.label: C
options.text: A describing word and a direction word can both follow the verb, and the describing word comes first; the pointing-back word *ai* comes after the direction word, as in *Sā nofo aʻe ai le tama*; and inside a spatial noun phrase the direction word comes after the belonging word and the thing the position is measured against.
options.explanation: Inside a spatial noun phrase the direction word comes directly after the spatial noun, before the belonging word.

options.label: D
options.text: A describing word and a direction word can both follow the verb, and the describing word comes first; the pointing-back word *ai* comes after the direction word, as in *Sā nofo aʻe ai le tama*; and inside a spatial noun phrase the direction word comes directly after the spatial noun, before the belonging word, as in *ʻi lalo ifo o le fale*.
options.explanation: Correct: the order after the verb is any describing word, then the direction word, then *ai*, and in *ʻi lalo ifo o le fale* the word *ifo* stands directly after *lalo* and before *o*.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of words linked to the direction words?

options.label: A
options.text: The direction word *ʻese* is the word for "far" doing a second job; the command word *ʻaumai* (bring) is an old verb of taking with *mai* fused onto its end; the compass nouns for east and west carry *aʻe* and *ifo*; and the spatial nouns for this side and the far side are *tala* with a direction word after it.
options.explanation: *ʻEse* is the word for "different, strange" doing a second job.

options.label: B
options.text: The direction word *ʻese* is the word for "different, strange" doing a second job; the command word *ʻaumai* (bring) is an old verb of taking with *atu* fused onto its end; the compass nouns for east and west carry *aʻe* and *ifo*; and the spatial nouns for this side and the far side are *tala* with a direction word after it.
options.explanation: *ʻAumai* carries *mai* inside it: take, toward me.

options.label: C
options.text: The direction word *ʻese* is the word for "different, strange" doing a second job; the command word *ʻaumai* (bring) is an old verb of taking with *mai* fused onto its end; the compass nouns for east and west carry *ifo* and *aʻe*, in that order; and the spatial nouns for this side and the far side are *tala* with a direction word after it.
options.explanation: The compass noun for east carries *aʻe*, up, and the one for west carries *ifo*, down, very likely from the rising and the setting of the sun.

options.label: D
options.text: The direction word *ʻese* is the word for "different, strange" doing a second job; the command word *ʻaumai* (bring) is an old verb of taking with *mai* fused onto its end; the compass nouns for east and west carry *aʻe* and *ifo*, in that order; and the spatial nouns for this side and the far side are *tala* with a direction word after it.
options.explanation: Correct: *sasaʻe* (east) holds *aʻe* and *sisifo* (west) holds *ifo*, and *tala mai* and *tala atu* are *tala* (next to) with a direction word after it.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of *aʻe* and *ifo*?

options.label: A
options.text: *Aʻe* is down and *ifo* is up; both are related to verbs of their own; a word of this pair can be followed by *mai*, *atu* or *ane*; and *aʻe* can carry a note of politeness, while *ifo* sometimes carries one of humility.
options.explanation: *Aʻe* is up and *ifo* is down, and neither takes its bearing from the speaker.

options.label: B
options.text: *Aʻe* is up and *ifo* is down; both are related to verbs of their own, *aʻe* go up, climb, and *ifo* bow down; a word of this pair cannot be followed by *mai*, *atu* or *ane*; and *aʻe* can carry a note of politeness, while *ifo* sometimes carries one of humility.
options.explanation: A word of this pair can be followed by *mai*, *atu* or *ane*, so one sentence can say both which way a thing went and whose way it was turned.

options.label: C
options.text: *Aʻe* is up and *ifo* is down; both are related to verbs of their own, *aʻe* go up, climb, and *ifo* bow down; a word of this pair can be followed by *mai*, *atu* or *ane*; and *ifo* can carry a note of politeness, while *aʻe* sometimes carries one of humility.
options.explanation: It is *aʻe* that can carry a note of politeness, and *ifo* that sometimes carries one of humility or self-abasement.

options.label: D
options.text: *Aʻe* is up and *ifo* is down; both are related to verbs of their own, *aʻe* go up, climb, and *ifo* bow down; a word of this pair can be followed by *mai*, *atu* or *ane*; and *aʻe* can carry a note of politeness, while *ifo* sometimes carries one of humility.
options.explanation: Correct: the pair stands in opposition and takes no bearing from the speaker, the two words are related to verbs of their own, and the two notes are hedged: *aʻe* can, *ifo* sometimes.

questions.prompt: The sentences *Na sau le tama mai le fale.* and *ʻOloʻo taʻoto mai le teine ʻi le fale.* both carry *mai*. Which of these is true?

options.label: A
options.text: In the first *mai* is the from-word; in the second it is the direction word, turning the action toward the speaker; and a direction word is used whether or not anything moves.
options.explanation: Correct: a place noun directly after *mai* makes it the from-word, and with the doer after it *mai* is the direction word, here on a girl who is lying still.

options.label: B
options.text: In both *mai* is the direction word, turning the action toward the speaker; and a direction word is used whether or not anything moves.
options.explanation: In the first a place noun follows *mai* directly, and that makes it the from-word: the boy came from the house.

options.label: C
options.text: In the first *mai* is the from-word; in the second it is the direction word, turning the action away from the speaker, toward the person spoken to; and a direction word is used whether or not anything moves.
options.explanation: The direction word *mai* turns the action toward the speaker, not away.

options.label: D
options.text: In the first *mai* is the from-word; in the second it is the direction word, turning the action toward the speaker; and a direction word is used only where something moves.
options.explanation: A direction word needs no movement: the girl is not moving at all, and *mai* says she lies where the speaker is, or turned the speaker's way.

31.title: The Complement Clause: Can and Must

questions.prompt: What do *faitalia*, *lavā*, *ulaula*, *pologa* and *uso* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: be able; do as one pleases; smoke; slave; sibling (a man's brother, a woman's sister)
options.explanation: The first two meanings are the wrong way round: *faitalia* is doing as one pleases, and *lavā* is being able.

options.label: B
options.text: do as one pleases; be able; smoke; slave; sibling (a man's brother, a woman's sister)
options.explanation: Correct: *lavā* is mostly met as *lē lavā*, cannot, and *uso* is a man's brother or a woman's sister.

options.label: C
options.text: do as one pleases; be able; slave; smoke; sibling (a man's brother, a woman's sister)
options.explanation: The third and fourth meanings are the wrong way round: *ulaula* is to smoke, and *pologa* is a slave.

options.label: D
options.text: do as one pleases; be able; smoke; sibling (a man's brother, a woman's sister); slave
options.explanation: The last two meanings are the wrong way round: *pologa* is a slave, and *uso* is a sibling.

questions.prompt: In *ʻUa tatau ona ʻou alu*, which part is the complement clause, and what is it?

options.label: A
options.text: The clause *ʻou alu* after *ona*: it fills the slot a noun phrase would fill for what the sentence is about, and *ona* is the that-word that opens it.
options.explanation: Correct: the clause after *ona* is what the sentence is about, and the word in front of it says something about that clause.

options.label: B
options.text: The clause *ʻou alu* after *ona*: it fills the slot of the doer, the one a phrase marked with *e* fills, and *ona* is the that-word that opens it.
options.explanation: The complement clause fills the slot for what the sentence is about, not the slot of a doer marked with *e*.

options.label: C
options.text: The clause *ʻou alu* after *ona*: it fills the slot a noun phrase would fill for what the sentence is about, and *ona* is a tense particle, the one that clause carries.
options.explanation: The word *ona* is the that-word, the joining word that opens the clause; it is not a tense particle.

options.label: D
options.text: The half in front of *ona*, *ʻUa tatau*: it fills the slot of the doer, and *ona* is the that-word that closes it.
options.explanation: The complement clause is the clause after *ona*, which opens it; on its own, *ʻUa tatau* is unfinished.

questions.prompt: Both *Sā lē mafai ona ʻou alu* and *E sā ona inu* carry *sā*. Which job does it do in each, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: The word for "forbidden" in the first, and the past particle in the second.
options.explanation: Both are the wrong way round: nothing stands in front of the first *sā*, and the general particle *e* stands in front of the second.

options.label: B
options.text: The past particle in both.
options.explanation: The second *sā* has the general particle *e* in front of it, so it stands in the predicate slot as the word for "forbidden".

options.label: C
options.text: The past particle in the first, and the word for "forbidden" in the second.
options.explanation: Correct: nothing stands in front of the first *sā* and the slot after it holds *lē mafai*, while the general particle *e* stands in front of the second.

options.label: D
options.text: The word for "forbidden" in both.
options.explanation: Nothing stands in front of the first *sā*, and the slot after it holds *lē mafai*, so it is the past particle.

questions.prompt: Translate into English: *ʻUa taga ona inu ʻava mālosi.*

options.label: A
options.text: It is forbidden to drink alcohol.
options.explanation: Forbidden would be *sā*; *taga* means allowed, may.

options.label: B
options.text: It is allowed to drink milk.
options.explanation: The words *ʻava mālosi* mean alcohol, strong kava, not milk.

options.label: C
options.text: It is forbidden to drink milk.
options.explanation: Here both words are misread: *taga* means allowed, and *ʻava mālosi* is alcohol.

options.label: D
options.text: It is allowed to drink alcohol.
options.explanation: Correct: *taga* is allowed, may, and *ʻava mālosi*, strong kava, is alcohol.

questions.prompt: How do you say "The girl can come" in Sāmoan?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻUa tatau ona sau le teine.*
options.explanation: This says the girl must come; *tatau* is the obligation word, necessary, must.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻUa mafai ona sau le teine.*
options.explanation: Correct: *mafai* is can, able, and the girl who can come stands inside the clause after *ona*.

options.label: C
options.text: *E sā ona sau le teine.*
options.explanation: This says it is forbidden for the girl to come; *sā* here is the word for forbidden, must not.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻUa iloa e le tama ʻua sau le teine.*
options.explanation: This says the boy knows that the girl has come; nothing in it says what she can do.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of *mafai* and the not-word *lē*?

options.label: A
options.text: The person can be named on *mafai* as well as inside the clause after *ona*, or inside that clause alone; and *lē* in front of *mafai* says the thing could not be done.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻOu te lē mafai ona ʻou ʻai meaʻai* names the person on both sides, *Sā lē mafai ona ʻou alu* only inside the clause, and in both *lē* makes the whole ability negative.

options.label: B
options.text: The person has to be named on *mafai* as well as inside the clause after *ona*; and *lē* in front of *mafai* says the thing could not be done.
options.explanation: In *Sā lē mafai ona ʻou alu*, *mafai* carries no person, and the clause alone says who would have gone.

options.label: C
options.text: The person can be named on *mafai* as well as inside the clause after *ona*, or inside that clause alone; and *lē* in front of *mafai* says a thing that could be done did not happen.
options.explanation: Placed in front of *mafai*, *lē* makes the whole ability negative: the thing was not possible.

options.label: D
options.text: The person has to be named on *mafai* as well as inside the clause after *ona*; and *lē* in front of *mafai* says a thing that could be done did not happen.
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: the person may be named inside the clause alone, and *lē* in front of *mafai* says the thing was not possible.

questions.prompt: What do *faʻasā* and *faʻataga* mean, in that order, and how are they built?

options.label: A
options.text: allow, and forbid; each is a word of its own, not built from *sā* or *taga*.
options.explanation: The meanings are the wrong way round, and the two words are built from *sā* and *taga*.

options.label: B
options.text: forbid, and allow; each is a word of its own, not built from *sā* or *taga*.
options.explanation: The meanings are right, but these are the maker-prefix at work on *sā* and *taga*.

options.label: C
options.text: allow, and forbid; each is the maker-prefix at work on *sā* and on *taga*.
options.explanation: The build is right, but the meanings are the wrong way round: *faʻasā* is to make forbidden, which is to forbid.

options.label: D
options.text: forbid, and allow; each is the maker-prefix at work on *sā* and on *taga*.
options.explanation: Correct: *sā* is forbidden and *faʻasā* is to forbid, while *taga* is allowed and *faʻataga* is to allow.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the words that take a clause after *ona*, such as *mafai* and *tatau*, as this chapter sets them in sentences?

options.label: A
options.text: Set in a sentence, each stands bare, with no tense particle of its own in front of it; it and the clause after *ona* name one event, which the word grades; and that clause always follows it.
options.explanation: Every one of these words set in a sentence in this chapter has a tense particle in front of it, as *e* stands in front of *tatau* in *E tatau ona alu le tama*.

options.label: B
options.text: Set in a sentence, each has a tense particle of its own in front of it; it and the clause after *ona* name two separate happenings, one each; and that clause always follows it.
options.explanation: There is one event, named by the clause after *ona*, and the word in front grades it as possible, necessary, permitted or forbidden.

options.label: C
options.text: Set in a sentence, each has a tense particle of its own in front of it; it and the clause after *ona* name one event, which the word grades; and that clause always follows it.
options.explanation: Correct: in *E tatau ona alu le tama* the particle *e* stands in front of *tatau*, the going is the one event, and the clause comes after.

options.label: D
options.text: Set in a sentence, each has a tense particle of its own in front of it; it and the clause after *ona* name one event, which the word grades; and that clause may also be put in front of it.
options.explanation: The complement clause always follows the word that takes it, and nothing puts it in front.

questions.prompt: A complement clause can be joined to the word that takes it in two ways: set down with nothing between, or opened by *ona*. Which of these is true of the tense particles, in the sentences this chapter shows?

options.label: A
options.text: Set down with nothing between, the clause carries no tense particle; opened by *ona*, it carries none either, and sits under the tense of the word in front.
options.explanation: The clause set down with nothing between keeps a tense particle of its own, as *ʻua sau* does in *ʻUa iloa e le tama ʻua sau le teine*.

options.label: B
options.text: Set down with nothing between, the clause keeps a tense particle of its own, read against the time of the first half; opened by *ona*, it carries none, and sits under the tense of the word in front.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻUa iloa e le tama ʻua sau le teine* carries two tense particles, and *ʻUa mafai ona sau le teine* carries one.

options.label: C
options.text: Set down with nothing between, the clause keeps a tense particle of its own, read against the time of the first half; opened by *ona*, it keeps a tense particle of its own as well.
options.explanation: A clause opened by *ona* never carries a tense particle, as the bare *sau* in *ʻUa mafai ona sau le teine* shows.

options.label: D
options.text: Set down with nothing between, the clause carries no tense particle; opened by *ona*, it keeps a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: This is the wrong way round: the clause with nothing between keeps its own tense particle, and the clause after *ona* carries none.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about *tatau* are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *tatau* was met earlier as "fit, proper"; with a clause after *ona*, it is the obligation word, necessary, must.
options.explanation: This is true: the obligation reading comes with the clause after *ona*.

options.label: B
options.text: The construction names no one who is doing the requiring; the person who has to act appears inside the clause after *ona*.

options.explanation: That reads *ʻoloʻo* against the moment of speaking; here the staying is placed at the time of the knowing, which is past, so it was going on then.

options.label: C
options.text: The boy knew that the girl was staying in the village.
options.explanation: Correct: the knowing is past, and *ʻoloʻo* puts the staying at the same time as the knowing.

options.label: D

questions.prompt: What does *Na iloa e loʻu ataliʻi ʻua sasae le ʻie.* mean, and which kind of possessive form does *ataliʻi* take?

options.label: B

options.explanation: The meaning is right, but *ataliʻi* takes an o-word possessive form: a father's son takes *o*.

options.label: C

options.explanation: Here *ʻua* marks the tearing as already done by the time of the knowing, not still to come.

options.label: D
options.text: My daughter knew that the cloth had been torn, and *ataliʻi* takes an o-word possessive form.
options.explanation: The word *ataliʻi* is a man's son, not a daughter.

questions.prompt: How do you say "The boy knows that the girl had stayed in the village"?

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻUa iloa e le tama sā nofo le teine ʻi le nuʻu.*

questions.prompt: In a reported clause, what do *ʻoleʻā* and the general particle *e* each do to the time of the reported event?

options.label: B
options.text: The particle *ʻoleʻā* puts it after the time of the report, and *e* puts it at the same time as the report.
options.explanation: Right about *ʻoleʻā*, but *e* sets no time of its own; *ʻoloʻo* is the particle that puts an event at the same time as the report.

options.label: C
options.text: The particle *ʻoleʻā* puts it after the moment of speaking, whatever time the report names, and *e* sets no time of its own.
options.explanation: Right about *e*, but *ʻoleʻā* is read against the time of the report, so under a past report it gives "would come", not a coming still ahead of now.

options.label: D
options.text: The particle *ʻoleʻā* puts it after the time of the report, and *e* sets no time of its own.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻoleʻā* marks an event still to come at the time of the report, and *e* sets no time of its own.

questions.prompt: Which word fills the gap in *Na fai mai le teine ___ alu le tama.* so that it means "The girl asked whether the boy would go"?

options.text: Position: the new *tā* stands between the tense particle and the verb or inside a possessive phrase, while the pronoun stands where the verb stands; it means tear.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true about reported commands and reported questions?

options.label: B

A reported question opens with a tense particle only, never with *pē* or *po*. With *faʻatonu*, the one who gives the order takes the agent marker *e*.
options.explanation: The first and last parts are right, but a reported question opens with *pē*, or with its other shape *po*.

options.label: C
options.text: A reported command opens with *ʻia*, which stands where a tense particle would otherwise stand, and the general particle *e* can stand there in its place. A reported question opens with *pē*, or with its other shape *po*. With *faʻatonu*, the one who gives the order stands after the verb with no marker.
options.explanation: The first two parts are right, but the one who gives the order takes the agent marker *e*, as *e le tama* does after *faʻatonu mai*.

options.text: A reported command opens with *ʻia*, which stands where a tense particle would otherwise stand, and the general particle *e* can stand there in its place. A reported question opens with *pē*, or with its other shape *po*. With *faʻatonu*, the one who gives the order takes the agent marker *e*.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about putting a phrase at the head of a sentence are true. Which one is false?

questions.prompt: What does *ʻO le leo o le pepe na lagona e le tinā.* mean?

questions.prompt: The sentence *Sā tapē e le tama le puaʻa.* can be said with either participant put first. Which is true when you do?

options.label: A
options.text: With either participant first the verb usually takes the long form *tapē=ina*, and this is a tendency rather than a rule.
options.explanation: Only a doer at the front leans toward the long form; a thing acted on at the front mostly keeps the short form *tapē*.

options.label: B
options.text: With the thing acted on first the verb mostly keeps the short form *tapē*, and the sentence reads two ways in English; with the doer first it usually takes the long form *tapē=ina*; both leanings are tendencies rather than rules.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻO le puaʻa sā tapē e le tama* is both "the boy killed the pig" and "the pig was killed by the boy", and *ʻO le tama sā tapē=ina le puaʻa* takes the long form, though usage varies from speaker to speaker.

options.label: C
options.text: With either participant first the verb mostly keeps the short form *tapē*, and this is a tendency rather than a rule.
options.explanation: Only a thing acted on at the front leans toward the short form; a doer at the front usually takes the long form *tapē=ina*.

options.label: D
options.text: With the thing acted on first the verb mostly keeps the short form *tapē*, and the sentence can only mean "the boy killed the pig"; with the doer first it usually takes the long form *tapē=ina*.
options.explanation: The shapes are right, but the sentence with the thing acted on first reads two ways in English, since Sāmoan does not choose between them.

questions.prompt: The words *lea* and *ia* can point back to a phrase put first. Which of these is true?

options.label: B
options.text: They point back to a thing acted on put first, *ia* for one thing and *lea* for more than one, and a doer put first can be said again by a middle-slot pronoun.

options.label: C
options.text: They point back to a doer put first, *lea* for one and *ia* for more than one, while a thing acted on put first can be said again by a middle-slot pronoun.

options.label: D

questions.prompt: Putting a phrase first does four jobs. Which of these statements about them is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Naming the topic: a phrase put first announces what the rest is going to be about. Contrast: two sentences side by side, each with its person at the front, set the two people against each other. Weight on one word: moving a phrase to the front marks it as the point of the sentence, with no word of emphasis added. The setting: a phrase saying where or when something happened can be put first.
options.explanation: Correct: these are the four jobs, and the third is done by the move alone, as in *ʻO le tama sā tapē=ina le puaʻa*, where no word of emphasis is added.

options.label: B
options.text: Naming the topic: a phrase put first hides what the rest is about, which is why Sāmoan stories so rarely open this way. Contrast: two sentences side by side, each with its person at the front, set the two people against each other. Weight on one word: moving a phrase to the front marks it as the point of the sentence, with no word of emphasis added. The setting: a phrase saying where or when something happened can be put first.
options.explanation: The first job is naming the topic: a phrase put first announces what the rest is about, which is why stories so often open this way.

options.label: C
options.text: Naming the topic: a phrase put first announces what the rest is going to be about. Contrast: two sentences side by side, each with its person at the front, say the same thing about both people and set nobody against anyone. Weight on one word: moving a phrase to the front marks it as the point of the sentence, with no word of emphasis added. The setting: a phrase saying where or when something happened can be put first.
options.explanation: Contrast does set the people against each other, as *ʻO aʻu na ʻou vaʻai ʻi ai* beside *ʻO ʻoe ʻe te leʻi vaʻai ʻi ai* sets the speaker against the listener.

options.label: D
options.text: Naming the topic: a phrase put first announces what the rest is going to be about. Contrast: two sentences side by side, each with its person at the front, set the two people against each other. Weight on one word: moving a phrase to the front marks it as the point of the sentence only when a word of emphasis is added as well. The setting: a phrase saying where or when something happened has to stay in its ordinary slot after the verb.
options.explanation: Wrong twice: the move alone marks the point of the sentence, and a phrase saying where or when can be put first.

questions.prompt: Which is true of the pointing-back word *ai* when a setting goes to the head of a sentence?

options.explanation: The setting presented by *ʻo* is still answered by the pointing-back word, as *ʻO le faʻatoʻaga sā galue ai le tama* shows.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true about the order of the naming sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: Only one order is good Sāmoan, and the other is wrong. The naming part nearly always carries *ʻo*, while the part being named carries *ʻo* only when it comes first. When the part being named is the speaker it comes first, and when it is a demonstrative such as *lenā* it must come second.
options.explanation: Both orders are good Sāmoan and say the same thing: *ʻO se uō le tama* and *ʻO le tama ʻo se uō* both mean "The boy is a friend", and which one a speaker picks is largely free.

options.label: B
options.text: Both orders are good Sāmoan and say the same thing, and which one a speaker picks is largely free. The naming part nearly always carries *ʻo*, while the part being named carries *ʻo* only when it comes first. When the part being named is the speaker it comes first, and when it is a demonstrative such as *lenā* it must come second.
options.explanation: Correct: that is why *ʻO le tama ʻo se uō* carries *ʻo* twice, why the chapter says *ʻO aʻu ʻo se uō* for "I am a friend", and why *ʻO le faleoʻo lenā* runs in that order.

options.label: C
options.text: Both orders are good Sāmoan and say the same thing, and which one a speaker picks is largely free. Both parts of the sentence carry *ʻo* wherever they stand. When the part being named is the speaker it comes first, and when it is a demonstrative such as *lenā* it must come second.
options.explanation: The naming part nearly always carries *ʻo*, but the part being named carries it only when it comes first, which is why *ʻO se uō le tama* has one *ʻo* and *ʻO le tama ʻo se uō* has two.

options.label: D
options.text: Both orders are good Sāmoan and say the same thing, and which one a speaker picks is largely free. The naming part nearly always carries *ʻo*, while the part being named carries *ʻo* only when it comes first. When the part being named is the speaker it comes last, and when it is a demonstrative such as *lenā* it can come first or second.

options.text: In *Na alu le tama, oso le teine ʻi le sami*, the *na* in front of the first clause sets the past for the second clause as well.
options.explanation: True: one tense particle at the front reaches over the whole run, so the jumping is past too.

options.label: B
options.text: Leaving the tense slot of the second clause empty says its event followed straight on from the first, or happened at the same time.
options.explanation: True: the empty slot is what ties the two clauses together.

options.label: C
options.text: The time a tense particle sets can reach on past a full stop into the next sentence.
options.explanation: True: a run of clauses does not have to stop where the full stop does.

options.label: D
options.text: In *Sā ʻou alu loa ʻi fafo. Fufulu oʻu mata.*, the second sentence names no one who washed, so who did it is left open.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because the *ʻou* of the first sentence says who washed, just as *sā* says when.

options.label: C
options.text: lie down; watch or look; move

options.label: D
options.text: forget; watch or look; speak
options.explanation: Speaking is *tautala*; the word *siʻi* is move.

questions.prompt: What does *E leʻi mafai ona ʻou alu leaga sā timu.* mean, and where is this use of *leaga* seldom met?

options.label: A
options.text: I could not go, and the rain was bad; in writing and formal language
options.explanation: Here *leaga* is not used as the word for bad but as a because-word, opening the reason for what was just said.

options.label: B
options.text: I could not go because luckily it was raining; in writing and formal language
options.explanation: The word *leaga* opens a reason that is a bad or unwelcome thing, so the reason cannot be a lucky one.

options.label: C
options.text: I could not go because unfortunately it was raining; in writing and formal language
options.explanation: Correct: *leaga* opens an unwelcome reason, and this use belongs to everyday speech, so it is seldom met in writing or formal language.

options.label: D
options.text: I could not go because unfortunately it was raining; in everyday speech
options.explanation: The meaning is right, but it is in everyday speech that this use of *leaga* belongs; it is the one seldom met in writing or formal language.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means "The boy went to bring the coconut"?

options.label: A
options.text: *Sā alu le tama e ʻaumai le niu.*
options.explanation: Correct: the general particle *e* heads the purpose clause, which says what the going was for.

options.label: B
options.text: *Sā ʻou alu neʻi tagi le tama.*
options.explanation: This says I went, so that the boy would not cry.

options.label: C
options.text: *Na alu le tama ʻi le fale ʻona ʻua maʻi le teine.*
options.explanation: This says the boy went to the house because the girl was sick, which gives a reason rather than a purpose.

options.label: D
options.text: *Sā ʻou alu ʻou te ʻaumai le niu.*
options.explanation: This says I went to bring the coconut; the one who went here is *ʻou*, not the boy.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the because-words and the clauses they open?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *ʻona* always comes after the main clause and never opens the sentence; when a reason is put first, the other clause usually carries *ai* after its verb; and a reason clause with a verb in it carries a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: The word *ʻona* can also go first, as in *ʻOna ʻua maʻi le teine, na alu ai le tama ʻi le fale.*

options.label: B
options.text: The word *ʻona* can open the sentence, in front of the main clause; when a reason is put first, the other clause usually carries *ai* after its verb; and a reason clause with a verb in it takes no tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: The reason clause carries a tense particle of its own, as *ʻua* does in *ʻua vāivai*.

options.label: C
options.text: The word *ʻona* can open the sentence, in front of the main clause; when a reason is put first, the other clause stays exactly as it would be, with nothing added; and a reason clause with a verb in it carries a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: When a reason goes first, the other clause usually carries the pointing-back word *ai* after its verb, reaching back to the whole reason.

options.label: D
options.text: The word *ʻona* can open the sentence, in front of the main clause; when a reason is put first, the other clause usually carries *ai* after its verb; and a reason clause with a verb in it carries a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻona* can go first, the other clause then usually takes *ai*, and the reason clause carries its own tense particle.

questions.prompt: Which of these is how this chapter tells you to read *ona* and *ʻona*?

options.label: A
options.text: A tense particle in front of the verb that follows marks the because-word, and no tense particle marks the that-word; the *ona* of the then-construction is told from the that-word by the *lea* that trails it; before a noun phrase the because-word takes the presenting particle *ʻo*; and in ordinary Sāmoan the two are usually both written *ona*, so the tense particle is the test.
options.explanation: Correct: the tense particle sorts the because-word from the that-word, the trailing *lea* sorts out the then-construction, *ʻo* stands between *ʻona* and a noun phrase, and the ʻ mark is usually not printed.

options.label: B
options.text: The ʻ mark marks the because-word, and ordinary Sāmoan writing always prints it, so the mark is the test; the *ona* of the then-construction is told from the that-word by the *lea* that trails it; and before a noun phrase the because-word takes the presenting particle *ʻo*.
options.explanation: In ordinary Sāmoan the two are usually both written *ona*, so the tense particle is the test to use.

options.label: C
options.text: A tense particle in front of the verb that follows marks the because-word, and no tense particle marks the that-word; the *ona* of the then-construction is told from the that-word by a tense particle in front of its verb; before a noun phrase the because-word takes the presenting particle *ʻo*; and in ordinary Sāmoan the two are usually both written *ona*, so the tense particle is the test.
options.explanation: The verb after the *ona* of the then-construction carries no tense particle either, so the trailing *lea* is what tells it apart.

options.label: D
options.text: A tense particle in front of the verb that follows marks the because-word, and no tense particle marks the that-word; the *ona* of the then-construction is told from the that-word by the *lea* that trails it; before a noun phrase the because-word stands straight in front of it, with nothing between; and in ordinary Sāmoan the two are usually both written *ona*, so the tense particle is the test.
options.explanation: Before a noun phrase *ʻona* takes the presenting particle, as in *ʻona ʻo le timu*.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true about purpose clauses?

options.label: A
options.text: After a preverbal pronoun the general particle stays *e* at the head of the purpose clause. *Neʻi* at its head makes the purpose negative, and a preverbal pronoun of the clause's own then comes after *neʻi*. The mood particle *ʻia* can head a purpose clause in place of *e*. A negative purpose clause can leave out the thing that is not to be noticed, when a sentence before it has already named that thing.
options.explanation: After a preverbal pronoun such as *ʻou* the general particle takes its other shape, *te*.

options.label: B
options.text: After a preverbal pronoun the general particle takes the shape *te* at the head of the purpose clause. *Neʻi* at its head makes the purpose negative, and a preverbal pronoun of the clause's own still stands in front of *neʻi*. The mood particle *ʻia* can head a purpose clause in place of *e*. A negative purpose clause can leave out the thing that is not to be noticed, when a sentence before it has already named that thing.
options.explanation: The pronoun moves behind *neʻi*, since the general particle is the only particle a pronoun stands in front of.

options.label: C
options.text: After a preverbal pronoun the general particle takes the shape *te* at the head of the purpose clause. *Neʻi* at its head makes the purpose negative, and a preverbal pronoun of the clause's own then comes after *neʻi*. The mood particle *ʻia* cannot head a purpose clause. A negative purpose clause must always name the thing that is not to be noticed again.
options.explanation: The mood particle *ʻia* can head a purpose clause in place of *e*, and the noticed thing can be left out when a sentence before has named it, as in *ʻUa ʻou ʻata ma ʻou punou ʻi lalo neʻi iloa mai e le tama.*

options.label: D
options.text: After a preverbal pronoun the general particle takes the shape *te* at the head of the purpose clause. *Neʻi* at its head makes the purpose negative, and a preverbal pronoun of the clause's own then comes after *neʻi*. The mood particle *ʻia* can head a purpose clause in place of *e*. A negative purpose clause can leave out the thing that is not to be noticed, when a sentence before it has already named that thing.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻou te* heads a purpose clause after a pronoun, *neʻi* turns it negative with the pronoun behind it, *ʻia* can stand in place of *e*, and the noticed thing can be left out once it has been named.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true about asking why and answering?

options.label: A
options.text: In the full why-question this chapter teaches, *ʻaiseā* stands at the end of its clause, and nothing in the verb phrase points back to it. *ʻAiseā* is used mainly on its own, as the one-word question, and the full why-sentence is heard in more formal language. *ʻAuā* and its reason can stand as the whole answer, with no main clause of their own.
options.explanation: In the full question *ʻaiseā* stands at the front of its clause, and *ai* in the verb phrase points back to it.

options.label: B
options.text: In the full why-question this chapter teaches, *ʻaiseā* stands at the front of its clause, and *ai* in the verb phrase points back to it. *ʻAiseā* is used mainly in the full why-sentence, and the one-word question is rare. *ʻAuā* and its reason can stand as the whole answer, with no main clause of their own.
options.explanation: The one-word question *ʻAiseā?* is the usual one, and the full sentence belongs to more formal language.

options.label: C
options.text: In the full why-question this chapter teaches, *ʻaiseā* stands at the front of its clause, and *ai* in the verb phrase points back to it. *ʻAiseā* is used mainly on its own, as the one-word question, and the full why-sentence is heard in more formal language. *ʻAuā* and its reason can stand as the whole answer, with no main clause of their own.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻAiseā?* is the usual question, and *ʻAuā ʻua maʻi le teine.* can be the whole of an answer.

options.label: D
options.text: In the full why-question this chapter teaches, *ʻaiseā* stands at the front of its clause, and *ai* in the verb phrase points back to it. *ʻAiseā* is used mainly on its own, as the one-word question, and the full why-sentence is heard in more formal language. An answer always needs a main clause of its own, so *ʻauā* and its reason cannot stand alone.
options.explanation: An answer needs no main clause of its own: *ʻAuā ʻua maʻi le teine.* can be the whole of it.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the because-words are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *ʻona* can open the sentence, in front of the main clause.
options.explanation: This is true: *ʻOna ʻua maʻi le teine, na alu ai le tama ʻi le fale.* opens on *ʻona*.

options.label: B
options.text: A reason clause with a verb in it carries a tense particle of its own, as *ʻua* does in *ʻua vāivai*.
options.explanation: This is true: the verb phrase after a because-word carries its own tense particle.

options.label: C
options.text: Before a noun phrase, *ʻona* takes the presenting particle *ʻo*.
options.explanation: This is true: *ʻona ʻo le timu* is "because of the rain".

options.label: D
options.text: A clause opened by *ʻauā* or *leaga* goes in front of the main clause as freely as a clause opened by *ʻona*.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: a clause opened by *ʻauā* normally comes after the main clause, and putting it first is rare, while *leaga* is not put first at all.

questions.prompt: Which word is the if-word, which word opens a condition clause with no if-word in front of it, and which written shape of that second word follows *pē*, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻāfai*, then *ʻoleʻā*, then *ʻā*

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻā*, then *ʻāfai*, then *ʻā*
options.explanation: The first two are the right words in the wrong order: *ʻāfai* is the if-word, and *ʻā* is the one that needs no if-word.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻāfai*, then *ʻā*, then the long shape *ʻā*, since the second written shape *ʻa* does not appear after *pē*
options.explanation: Correct: the short future particle has a second written shape, *ʻa*, and what decides between the two is not known, but after the question opener only the long shape appears.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻāfai*, then *ʻā*, then the second shape *ʻa*
options.explanation: The words are right, but after *pē* only the long shape *ʻā* appears.

questions.prompt: What does *ʻĀfai e mālosi le loto o le tama, e lē usitaʻi* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: If the boy's will is strong, he does not obey.
options.explanation: Correct: the if-word opens the condition, *loto* is the will, and *usitaʻi* is obey, here under the not-word.

options.label: B
options.text: If the boy's voice is strong, he does not obey.
options.explanation: The word *loto* means will or heart, not voice.

options.label: C
options.text: If the boy's will is strong, he does not sleep.
options.explanation: The word *usitaʻi* means obey, not sleep.

options.label: D
options.text: If the boy does not obey, his will is strong.
options.explanation: The condition is the clause the if-word opens, the boy's strong will, and not obeying is what follows from it.

questions.prompt: What does *ʻĀ ʻe alu ʻi le matāfaga, ʻaumai le solo* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: When you go to the market, you bring the towel.

options.label: B
options.text: When you go to the beach, bring the towel.
options.explanation: Correct: *matāfaga* is the beach, and the main clause behind the condition is a command.

options.label: C
options.text: When you go to the market, bring the towel.
options.explanation: The command is right, but *matāfaga* is the beach.

options.label: D
options.text: When you go to the beach, you bring the towel.
options.explanation: The place is right, but the main clause *ʻaumai le solo* is a command, "bring the towel", and not a statement of what you do.

questions.prompt: What does *E lē alu le malaga pē ʻā afā* mean, and what chooses between "when" and "if" in the English?

options.label: A
options.text: There will be no trip, whether or not there is a storm; the Sāmoan marks which English word fits.
options.explanation: Here the clause after *pē* is a condition, not the whether of a reported question.

options.label: B
options.text: There will be no trip when there is a fire; the Sāmoan does not mark the difference, so the translator chooses.
options.explanation: Both halves of the meaning are off: the clause after *pē* is a condition, and *afā* is a storm, not a fire.

options.label: C
options.text: There will be no trip when there is a storm; the Sāmoan marks which English word fits.
options.explanation: The meaning is right, but the Sāmoan does not mark whether the English should say "if", "when" or "whenever".

options.label: D
options.text: There will be no trip when there is a storm; the Sāmoan does not mark the difference among "if", "when" and "whenever", so the choice is the translator's.
options.explanation: Correct: the clause after *pē* is a condition, *afā* is a storm, and the choice of English word is the translator's.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a correct Sāmoan way to say "There will be no trip if it rains tomorrow"?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻĀ e timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.*
options.explanation: The short future particle is itself the tense particle of its clause, so a second one, *e*, has no place behind it.

options.label: B
options.text: *E lē alu le malaga ʻāfai e timu taeao.*
options.explanation: A condition clause that follows the main clause takes the question opener in front of it, so this needs *pē ʻāfai*.

options.label: C
options.text: *E lē alu le malaga pē ʻāfai e timu taeao.*
options.explanation: Correct: the condition follows the main clause, so the question opener *pē* stands in front of the if-word, and the verb *timu* carries the general particle *e*.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻĀfai timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.*
options.explanation: The clause after the if-word has a verb, *timu*, and a verb there carries a tense particle of its own, which is missing here, as in *ʻĀfai e timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.*

questions.prompt: In *ʻĀfai ʻua sau le tama, ʻoleʻā alu le teine* and *ʻĀfai ʻoleʻā timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga*, what does the tense particle of each condition say about it, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: In the first, that the speaker is not sure it will come true; in the second, that it is much more certain than under the general particle, as something expected soon.
options.explanation: The second is right, but *ʻua* presents the condition as something new that has come about; not being sure is a reading of the general particle *e*.

options.label: B
options.text: In the first, that it is something new that has come about; in the second, that it is much more certain than under the general particle, as something expected soon.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻua* presents the condition as something new that has come about, and *ʻoleʻā* points at something expected to happen soon.

options.label: C
options.text: In the first, that it is much more certain than under the general particle; in the second, that it is something new that has come about.
options.explanation: These are the right two readings in the wrong order: *ʻua* is the one for something new, and *ʻoleʻā* the one for greater certainty.

options.label: D
options.text: In the first, that it is something new that has come about; in the second, that it is less certain than under the general particle, though still something expected soon.
options.explanation: The first is right, but *ʻoleʻā* carries a much higher degree of certainty than the general particle does, not a lower one.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true about condition clauses?

options.label: A
options.text: A clause opened by *ʻā* only ever looks ahead to something still to come, never back into the past. A naming sentence opened by *ʻo* can stand as the condition, with no verb in it at all. Under the general particle *e*, one condition can mean that the speaker is not sure it will come true, or can mean "whenever" it is given. A condition clause standing in front of the main clause is occasionally opened by *pē* as well.
options.explanation: The shape can also look back into the past, as in *ʻĀ fānau mai le ulugāliʻi, e fiafia le ʻāiga*, "When the couple had children, the family was happy".

options.label: B
options.text: A clause opened by *ʻā* can also look back into the past. A condition clause must always have a verb in it, so a naming sentence cannot stand as the condition. Under the general particle *e*, one condition can mean that the speaker is not sure it will come true, or can mean "whenever" it is given. A condition clause standing in front of the main clause is occasionally opened by *pē* as well.
options.explanation: A naming sentence opened by *ʻo* can stand as the condition, as in *ʻĀfai ʻo le tonu, ʻua lelei*, with no verb in it at all.

options.label: C
options.text: A clause opened by *ʻā* can also look back into the past. A naming sentence opened by *ʻo* can stand as the condition, with no verb in it at all. Under the general particle *e*, one condition can mean that the speaker is not sure it will come true, or can mean "whenever" it is given. A condition clause standing in front of the main clause is occasionally opened by *pē* as well.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻĀ fānau mai le ulugāliʻi* looks back, *ʻĀfai ʻo le tonu, ʻua lelei* has a naming sentence as its condition, *ʻĀfai e timu, e lē alu le malaga* carries both readings, and *pē* can occasionally open a condition in front of the main clause, though the usual shape has nothing in front of the if-word or the short future particle.

options.label: D
options.text: A clause opened by *ʻā* can also look back into the past. A naming sentence opened by *ʻo* can stand as the condition, with no verb in it at all. Under the general particle *e*, one condition can only mean that the speaker is sure it will come true. A condition clause standing in front of the main clause is never opened by *pē*.
options.explanation: Under the general particle *e* a condition can mean that the speaker is not sure, or "whenever", and nothing in the Sāmoan chooses between them; and *pē* does occasionally open a condition in front of the main clause.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the particles of this chapter are true. Which one is false?

options.label: B
options.text: The short future particle has a second written shape, *ʻa*, and what decides between the two shapes is not known.
options.explanation: This is true: mostly the two look like free alternatives.

options.explanation: This is true: after the question opener only the long shape appears, as in *E lē alu le malaga pē ʻā afā*.

options.label: D
options.text: This chapter teaches *ʻā* as a fourth tense particle that can stand behind *ʻāfai*, beside *e*, *ʻua* and *ʻoleʻā*.
options.explanation: Correct: behind the if-word this chapter teaches three tense particles, and *ʻā* belongs to the other shape, standing where the if-word and its tense particle would be.

questions.prompt: What do *faigatā*, *faigōfie*, *taugatā*, *taugōfie*, *maugatā* and *maugōfie* mean, in that order?

options.text: difficult, easy, cheap, expensive, mean, generous
